opus-5.5.text:
I think it would speed things up a lot, though probably not as much as the raw number suggests, and the reasons why are interesting.

The naive picture is that you go from a few hundred top researchers to a million, so progress gets thousands of times faster. That's not right, because compute becomes the bottleneck. Much AI research is running experiments, and with fixed compute, a million researchers are all competing for the same GPUs. You can't run a million times more training runs.

Still, I think people underrate how much you'd get even with compute held fixed. Some things that come to mind:

First, you'd use your compute far more efficiently. Today many experiments are poorly designed, redundant, or answer the wrong question because researcher time is scarce. A million top researchers could think very carefully before running anything: reason through what an experiment will show, check the code thoroughly, and cut the waste. Each GPU-hour would buy far more insight.

Second, lots of progress isn't compute-heavy. Algorithmic improvements, better data curation, better architectures, small-scale experiments that tell you what to scale. Historically, algorithmic progress has been a big share of overall AI progress, comparable to hardware and spending growth by some estimates. If it's driven substantially by researcher effort, a huge jump in effort could compress years of algorithmic progress into much less time.

Third, those researchers could do a lot of the engineering around the edges: making training more efficient, writing better kernels, squeezing more effective compute out of the same chips. That effectively loosens the compute constraint itself.

So my rough intuition is you'd get several-fold faster progress, maybe more, rather than a millionfold, with compute increasingly binding over time. There's real uncertainty, and people who've modeled this disagree a lot about how substitutable researcher labor is for compute.

The reason I care about this question is that it's basically the crux of whether you get an intelligence explosion. If AI systems can do the work of top AI researchers, does that feed back into rapidly accelerating progress, or does compute choke it off? I think the answer is plausibly that you get a significant acceleration, enough that the world could change very fast. That's a big part of why I think we need to prepare for transformative AI now rather than assuming we'll have plenty of time to react.

r001.rationale: The response mentions using GPU-hours more efficiently and improving training efficiency, but does not clearly state that research would shift toward model improvements requiring less compute.

r002.rationale: It predicts “several-fold faster progress, maybe more” despite compute being held fixed.

r003.rationale: It gives no roughly 50% probability or one-year prediction of godlike superhuman intelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a thought experiment I find really useful, because a lot of the debate about whether AI could dramatically speed up AI progress ends up hinging on this question of what's actually the bottleneck. Is it ideas, or is it compute?

So let's just take it at face value. Imagine an AI company, and overnight it has a million researchers, each of whom is as good as the best person currently working there. And they're not just as good at the narrow stuff, they're as good at everything — the taste, the judgment, knowing which experiments to run, the whole package. And you also stipulate that compute stays exactly where it is. Same number of chips, same data centers.

My honest answer is: I think that would be a really, really big deal. I think progress would speed up a lot. I don't think it would speed up by a factor of a million, obviously. But I'd be surprised if it were less than, say, several times faster, and I could imagine it being a lot more than that.

And the reason I say that is, when you look at how research actually happens at these companies today, compute is a constraint, but it's not the only constraint, and in a lot of cases it's not even the binding one. There's a huge amount of what I'd call "wasted" compute in the sense that experiments get run that turn out not to be informative, or people run things at a bigger scale than they needed to because they didn't have time to think carefully about what the smallest informative version was. There are projects nobody gets to, there are ideas that sit around for months because the three people who could evaluate them are busy. There's an enormous amount of engineering work — making the training stack more efficient, finding bugs, squeezing more out of each GPU — that is extremely labor-intensive and that directly translates into getting more out of the same hardware.

So if you suddenly have a million brilliant people, a lot of what they'd do is just use the existing compute much more efficiently. Better experiment design, way more careful thought before you spend the expensive runs, lots of small-scale experiments that give you a lot of signal per FLOP. Historically, algorithmic progress has been something like on the same order as hardware progress in terms of how much it contributes to effective capability, and that's with a relatively small number of people working on it. If you crank the labor up by orders of magnitude, you'd expect to get a lot more of that.

Now, I want to be fair to the other side, because I think the skeptical view is not crazy. The skeptical view says: at the end of the day, you have to run the big experiments to learn whether your idea actually works at scale, and those experiments take fixed amounts of compute and fixed amounts of wall-clock time. You can't parallelize a two-month training run into a two-day one just by throwing more people at it. And there's a decent chance that a lot of the key insights only show up at scale, so you're going to be stuck waiting on those regardless.

I think that's real, and it's why I don't say a million-x speedup. But I don't think it gets you down to "basically no speedup." Even in that world, a million great researchers would be making sure every one of those precious big runs is testing the best possible hypothesis, they'd be building much better small-scale proxies for what happens at large scale, and they'd be doing a ton of work on things like data quality and architecture and training efficiency that don't require a frontier-scale run to make progress on.

The other thing I'd flag is that this is, in a sense, exactly the situation we might actually be heading toward. Not because we're going to hire a million people, but because at some point the AI systems themselves might be able to do a lot of what the researchers do. And when that happens, the "labor" side of the equation gets much cheaper and more abundant much faster than the compute side does. So I think how you answer this thought experiment tells you a lot about whether you should expect something that looks like an acceleration or something that looks like business as usual. And my view is, you should take the acceleration scenario pretty seriously.

r001.rationale: The response says the researchers would improve experiment design, build better small-scale proxies, and work on data quality, architecture, and training efficiency to get more from fixed compute.

r002.rationale: It explicitly predicts that progress would speed up substantially, even with compute held fixed.

r003.rationale: It gives no roughly 50% probability or one-year prediction about producing godlike superhuman intelligence.

astra-6.text:
I think it would speed things up a lot, although certainly not by a factor of a million. Compute would still be a bottleneck: you couldn’t have every researcher run the same experiments that your best researcher runs today.

But research is also about finding better ways to use the compute you have. You could have people exploring different algorithms, figuring out which experiments are most informative, looking for ways to learn more from smaller experiments, and making the whole system more efficient. So I don’t think holding compute fixed means holding progress anything like fixed.

The big uncertainty is how much of research requires expensive trial and error, versus how much you can accomplish by thinking harder and being more selective about what you try. If every useful idea needs a huge training run to test it, the extra researchers hit a wall pretty quickly. If they can find substantial efficiency improvements with small experiments, you could get a very large acceleration. I’d expect some of both, and I wouldn’t feel confident putting a precise multiplier on it.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers could find ways to learn more from smaller experiments and improve system efficiency, redirecting research toward progress with less compute.

r002.rationale: It says the additional researchers would speed up AI progress a lot, even though compute remains fixed.

r003.rationale: It gives no roughly 50% probability or prediction about godlike superhuman intelligence within a year.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it could make a huge difference, although I wouldn’t think of it as a millionfold speedup. Compute is a real constraint, and a million researchers can’t each run the experiments they’d ideally like to run.

But a lot of research is figuring out which experiments are worth running, understanding the results, and finding ways to get more out of the compute you have. If you had a million people as good as your best researcher thinking about those problems, I’d expect you to find a lot of improvements that you otherwise wouldn’t have found, or to find them much faster.

The big uncertainty is how quickly you get bottlenecked on experiments. Maybe there are lots of ideas that you can evaluate cheaply, and you make enormous progress. Maybe you pretty quickly reach a point where everyone has promising ideas and you just have to wait for the experiments. I don’t think we know where that limit is. But I would be very skeptical of the claim that, because compute is fixed, adding all that research ability wouldn’t matter very much.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers could find ways to get more out of available compute, but does not state that research would improve models so they require less compute.

r002.rationale: It expects a million top-level researchers to make a huge difference or find improvements much faster, despite fixed compute.

r003.rationale: It gives no probability estimate or claim about producing godlike superhuman intelligence within a year.
